title: Chablis and the Mâconnais
subtitle: North and south
objectives: Describe the Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais

steps.title: Chablis
steps.body: Chablis, isolated in the north, about 130 km from Dijon, is cooler than the Côte d'Or. Chardonnay grows on Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of tiny oyster fossils. Wines are lean, mineral and high in acidity. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and seven Grand Cru climats, like Les Clos and Valmur, on one south-west facing slope.

steps.title: Chalonnaise and Mâconnais
steps.body: South of the Côte d'Or, the Côte Chalonnaise has villages like Mercurey and Givry for reds, and Rully and Montagny for whites, offering good value. The Mâconnais, further south and warmer, makes rounder Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages, and Pouilly-Fuissé, which gained Premier Cru vineyards in 2020, and Saint-Véran.

steps.prompt: What makes Chablis' Kimmeridgian soil distinctive?
options: It's full of tiny oyster fossils
steps.explanation: Kimmeridgian marl contains countless fossilised oyster shells.

steps.title: Comparing whites
steps.body: Chablis is lean and mineral, usually unoaked or lightly oaked. The Côte de Beaune is richer, with oak. The Mâconnais is rounder, fruitier and more affordable. All are Chardonnay, showing how much place and climate change it.

steps.prompt: Which are Mâconnais or Chalonnaise wines?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chablis is lean and mineral on Kimmeridgian soil
The Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais offer value
